sections.text: Isaiah brings words of judgment and of hope to Judah and Jerusalem. The first part (chapters 1 to 39) warns of the consequences of injustice and false trust, and promises a child who will rule on David’s throne. The second part (40 to 55) comforts a people in exile and speaks of a servant who suffers for others. The last part (56 to 66) looks ahead to a renewed people and a new heavens and a new earth.

Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem in the second half of the eighth century before Christ, during the Assyrian threat. Many scholars think chapters 40 to 66 come from later prophets in his tradition, during and after the exile. Others hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book.

The New Testament quotes Isaiah more than any other prophet. Christians read the servant of chapter 53 as fulfilled in the death of Jesus. Jewish interpretation has most often understood the servant as Israel. Passages such as 7:14 and 9:6 are read by Christians as pointing to Christ, while also having a meaning in Isaiah’s own day.
